items.title: [Perspectives] Horology and the heart
items.summary: At the turn of the 17th century, the Venetian physician Santorio Santorio (1561–1636) described an instrument that rendered the pulse measurable. A weight was hung from a cord against a graduated scale and set swinging, the cord lengthened or shortened until the swing matched the beat beneath the doctor's fingers; a reading could then be taken from the scale. Santorio named it the pulsilogium, one of the first instruments of precision in medicine. Until then the pulse had been read by touch. items.title: Impact of high versus low fraction of inspired oxygen for anaesthetic washout and extubation on postoperative pulmonary atelectasis formation and oxygenation: importance of cumulative perioperative oxygen exposure. Comment on Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 591–600
items.summary: We read with interest the study by Paschold and colleagues1 showing that using a fraction of inspired oxygen (Fio2) of 70% for anaesthetic washout before extubation reduces postoperative pulmonary atelectasis and maintains oxygenation after tracheal extubation. We commend the authors for studying Fio2 management during emergence from general anaesthesia, a phase that is often overlooked, and for offering anaesthetists practical guidance on perioperative oxygen strategies. However, given the design of the study, some of the findings should be interpreted with caution.

As part of this evolution and in response to the Difficult Airway Society (DAS) 2025 guidelines for managing unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation in adults,1 we propose that in certain areas this trolley is no longer necessary.

items.title: From population targets to personalised titration: translating within-patient electroencephalographic responses into clinical practice
items.summary: Population-derived target ranges of drug concentrations or EEG indices are commonly used in clinical practice for the titration of anaesthesia. By definition, this inevitably results in a relative overdose for most patients and an underdose for a few. For accurate individualised titration of anaesthesia, suitable within-subject targets need to be established. For this reason, we identified multicentre trials powered for clinical endpoints and long-term cognitive outcomes as a priority for future research.

items.title: Global Surgery and Anaesthesia—A Short Guide to Meaningful Involvement
items.summary: In recent years, contemporary armed conflicts have multiplied in number, intensity, and duration, resulting in ever-increasing human losses. Climate-change-associated natural disasters are becoming more frequent and devastating. Epidemics, whether global or localised, such as the recurring Ebola outbreaks, regularly highlight the fragility of health systems. In many parts of the world, treatable diseases continue to cause preventable deaths due to a lack of resources, qualified personnel, or organised healthcare.

items.title: Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: A Practical Approach
items.summary: Critical care medicine has always been written in chapters. Some of its most influential textbooks have focused on the great syndromes and technologies that transformed our ability to save lives, and each has contributed to the extraordinary progress of modern intensive care. Yet, despite their importance, these textbooks often leave one fundamental question unanswered: what happens after survival?

items.title: Postoperative hypotension in patients recovering from noncardiac surgery: from detection to clinically meaningful interpretation. Response to Br J Anaesth 2026; 137: 1846-7
items.summary: We thank Wu and colleagues1 for their thoughtful comments on our observational study on postoperative hypotension in patients recovering from noncardiac surgery.2 Hypotension is a clinical sign. We agree that not all hypotension is equal; as with intraoperative hypotension,3,4 different endotypes of postoperative hypotension could exist with varying clinical importance. Nocturnal dipping, a decrease in blood pressure at night, is a sign of good long-term cardiovascular health rather than a risk factor for organ injury.
